title: J.P. Morgan Asset Management enters managed futures ETF market with JPFP - Alternatives Watch
content: Travis Spence, global head of ETFs at J.P. Morgan Asset Management (Photo credit: J.P. Morgan Asset Management) J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched the JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF on the NASDAQ, bringing a combined equity-and-managed-futures strategy to retail investors through a single fund as allocators increasingly look to the asset class for portfolio diversification in 2026. The fund, trading under the ticker JPFP, pairs a U.S. equity sleeve — providing broad exposure to large-cap stocks through direct holdings or equity index futures — with a managed futures component that uses proprietary models to take long and short positions across global equities, fixed income, currencies, and commodities. The launch arrives against a backdrop of renewed institutional interest in managed futures. PivotalPath indices flagged the strategy as the top-performing hedge fund category in the first quarter of 2026, with gains of 4.6%. Industry practitioners interviewed by Alternatives Watch have flagged the strategy as a standout diversifier for the year, including Jason Hubschman, co-COO and co-head of Alternative Managed Accounts at Wilshire, and Nate Garrison, senior vice president and CIO of World Investment Advisors. In February, Mast Investments CIO Yung Shin Kung told AW that his systematic investment firm had managed futures ETFs in registration with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. "Managed futures have historically shown low correlation to both stocks and bonds, suitable for advisors looking for ways to diversify beyond traditional portfolios," said Travis Spence, global head of ETFs at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. Based in London, Spence ascended to the role in August 2024 after a 20-year career at J.P. Morgan Asset Management that included serving as head of EMEA ETF distribution and leading the firm's Fixed Income Investment Specialist team. "JPFP reflects our commitment to expanding our active ETF offering, giving clients a simple way to incorporate a source of diversification into their portfolios using an ETF wrapper," added Spence. JPFP is managed by the Quantitative Solutions team, part of J.P. Morgan Asset Management's $529 billion Multi-Asset Solutions group. The portfolio management team is led by Dr. Yazann Romahi, CIO for Quantitative Solutions, alongside Kartik Aiyar, Dr. Wei Li and Garrett Norman. "JPFP brings an approach we have used extensively in our multi-asset portfolios to individual investors in an ETF," Romahi said. "It's designed to complement portfolios across market cycles by helping investors maintain equity exposure while adding a managed futures strategy for diversification, especially during periods when traditional asset classes face headwinds." Morgan Securities had claimed that the platter was served at a personal Super Bowl party. According to that same attorney, Marc Seldin Rosen, the platter had been purchased for a “pre-approved business meeting.” ​The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority ruled that the company must pay Bodner the sum of $4,250,000 in compensatory damages, according to FINRA documents. The ruling states that the firm must pay interest on the huge sum at the rate of 10 percent each year from the date of service until the award is paid. ​ The FINRA also ruled that J.P. Morgan Securities must repay Bodner an $800 for the non-refundable portion of a filing fee. In addition, the organization recommended that the reason for Bodner’s departure should be revised to “voluntary,” and that the “Termination Explanation should be deleted in its entirety.”​ Rosen told People that Bodner was fired back in 2024, after the company raised concerns over the deli platter, which he charged to the firm, that they claimed was for a personal event. The lawyer added that Bodner’s assistant had sought approval for the food order in advance. ​ “I'm unsurprised,” Rosen told the magazine, referring to the ruling. “And I was hopeful that it would be more in line with the actual damages he sustained, but given the forum we were in, you can't disrespect that outcome.” The lawyer confirmed that his client now works for Wells Fargo. ​However, a spokesperson for JP Morgan said that the company is “disappointed by the outcome.” ​ “We vehemently disagree with FINRA's decision and are disappointed by this outcome,” a spokesperson for the firm told The Independent. “We disagree with counsel’s characterizations of the facts and believe they are contrary to the witness testimony and evidence presented at the hearing.”​ “In every workplace in America, submitting an inaccurate expense report is grounds for termination,” the spokesperson continued. “When a company takes reasonable actions based on its investigation and submits a good faith U5 in compliance with the law, it should not be second-guessed and punished with a multi-million-dollar award.” “An internal review found that the claimant obtained preapproval to take a “client” (the advisor’s cousin) and the client’s boyfriend (purportedly a business prospect) to dinner at a local deli,” the spokesperson claimed. “Instead, the advisor held a Super Bowl party at his home for family and friends, including the cousin and boyfriend. “He then submitted the receipt for food from the deli for over a dozen people as a business expense,” the spokesperson concluded. “Thus, he both misstated the purpose and location of the gathering, which violated the firm’s policies. “The advisor, as an at-will employee, was therefore terminated for breaching the company’s trust and misusing their position.” Speaking to The New York Post, Rosen said that the paperwork for the platter had been handled by Bodner’s assistant in the same way in which she had made similar food orders in the past.​ “They weren’t hiding anything,” he said, stating that a receipt showed delivery to his client’s home. “There was nothing nefarious at all. They submitted the documents showing that it was at his house.”​ According to Rosen, the assistant coded the expense as though it had been consumed at the deli rather than delivered to Bodner’s home. However, he claims that the charge fell below the firm’s spending cap and complied with company policy at the time. ​ The Independent has contacted JPMorgan and Marc Seldin Rosen for comment. title: J.P. Morgan Asset Management Launches JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF (JPFP) on Nasdaq - PR Newswire

Morgan Asset Management Launches JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF (JPFP) on NYSE, issued 28-May-2026 by J.P. Morgan Asset Management over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that the exchange for the ETF should be: "Nasdaq." The complete, corrected release follows: New active ETF expands lineup, leveraging the expertise of the firm's Multi-Asset Solutions platform NEW YORK, May 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- J.P. Morgan Asset Management today announced the launch of the JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF (NASDAQ: JPFP) on the Nasdaq Stock Market, expanding the firm's active ETF platform and reinforcing its position as one of the leaders in the global active ETF space1. The new actively managed multi-asset ETF seeks to provide long-term capital appreciation and diversification beyond traditional stocks and bonds. JPFP is designed to give investors access to both U.S. equities and a managed futures strategy in a single, integrated fund structure. JPFP can offer low to at times negative correlation to equity and fixed income, which may provide a smoother investment journey and lower drawdown without altering an investor's existing portfolio. The fund's managed futures sleeve uses proprietary models to take long and short positions across global equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities. The U.S. equity sleeve provides broad exposure to large-cap U.S. stocks and may be implemented through a mix of direct equity holdings and/or equity index futures. "Managed futures have historically shown low correlation to both stocks and bonds, suitable for advisors looking for ways to diversify beyond traditional portfolios," said Travis Spence, Global Head of ETFs, J.P. Morgan Asset Management. "JPFP reflects our commitment to expanding our active ETF offering, giving clients a simple way to incorporate a source of diversification into their portfolios using an ETF wrapper." JPFP is managed by the Quantitative Solutions team, which is part of J.P. Morgan Asset Management's $529 billion Multi-Asset Solutions group2. The portfolio management team includes Dr. Yazann Romahi, PhD, CFA, Chief Investment Officer for Quantitative Solutions, Kartik Aiyar, Dr. Wei (Victor) Li, and Garrett Norman. Together, the team brings decades of experience designing and applying systematic macro models, and they are supported by quantitative and fundamental researchers with cross-asset expertise. "JPFP brings an approach we have used extensively in our multi-asset portfolios to individual investors in an ETF," said Dr. Romahi. "It's designed to complement portfolios across market cycles by helping investors maintain equity exposure while adding a managed futures strategy for diversification, especially during periods when traditional asset classes face headwinds." 1Source: Bloomberg, Factset. Cash flow can come from bond interest, interest from other types of investments, and, of course, dividends. A dividend is that coveted distribution of a company's earnings paid out to shareholders, and investors often view it by its dividend yield, a metric that measures the dividend as a percent of the current stock price. title: J.P. Morgan Asset Management Launches JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF (JPFP) on NYSE - Yahoo! Finance Canada
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results New active ETF expands lineup, leveraging the expertise of the firm's Multi-Asset Solutions platform NEW YORK, May 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- J.P. Morgan Asset Management today announced the launch of the JPMorgan Managed Futures Plus ETF (NYSE: JPFP) on the New York Stock Exchange, expanding the firm's active ETF platform and reinforcing its position as one of the leaders in the global active ETF space1. The new actively managed multi-asset ETF seeks to provide long-term capital appreciation and diversification beyond traditional stocks and bonds. JPFP is designed to give investors access to both U.S. equities and a managed futures strategy in a single, integrated fund structure. JPFP can offer low to at times negative correlation to equity and fixed income, which may provide a smoother investment journey and lower drawdown without altering an investor's existing portfolio. The fund's managed futures sleeve uses proprietary models to take long and short positions across global equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities. The U.S. equity sleeve provides broad exposure to large-cap U.S. stocks and may be implemented through a mix of direct equity holdings and/or equity index futures. "Managed futures have historically shown low correlation to both stocks and bonds, suitable for advisors looking for ways to diversify beyond traditional portfolios," said Travis Spence, Global Head of ETFs, J.P. Morgan Asset Management. "JPFP reflects our commitment to expanding our active ETF offering, giving clients a simple way to incorporate a source of diversification into their portfolios using an ETF wrapper." JPFP is managed by the Quantitative Solutions team, which is part of J.P. Morgan Asset Management's $529 billion Multi-Asset Solutions group2. The portfolio management team includes Dr. Yazann Romahi, PhD, CFA, Chief Investment Officer for Quantitative Solutions, Kartik Aiyar, Dr. Wei (Victor) Li, and Garrett Norman. Together, the team brings decades of experience designing and applying systematic macro models, and they are supported by quantitative and fundamental researchers with cross-asset expertise. "JPFP brings an approach we have used extensively in our multi-asset portfolios to individual investors in an ETF," said Dr. Romahi. "It's designed to complement portfolios across market cycles by helping investors maintain equity exposure while adding a managed futures strategy for diversification, especially during periods when traditional asset classes face headwinds." 1Source: Bloomberg, Factset. title: JPMorgan's Costs Could Hit $106 Billion As Wall Street Revenue Rises - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase JPM is heading into the rest of the year with a higher cost outlook, but CEO Jamie Dimon framed the increase as the byproduct of stronger business momentum. Speaking at the Bernstein Strategic Decisions Conference, Dimon said the bank's full-year costs will probably be closer to $106 billion than the $105 billion guidance executives had reaffirmed in April, with the additional $1 billion mostly tied to better performance across key Wall Street businesses. The pressure is coming from a place investors may not want to ignore: stronger trading and investment-banking activity. Dimon said markets revenue for the quarter ending June 30 could rise 11% from a year earlier, or possibly more, while investment-banking fees are expected to climb 10% and could come in slightly better depending on how the quarter finishes. That strength also means higher compensation and transaction-related costs, as traders and dealmakers tend to be paid in line with the revenue they generate. Still, the market reaction showed investors were weighing the higher expense base carefully. JPMorgan shares fell about 2.8% to $298.07 at 11:31 a.m. in New York Wednesday, making the bank the weakest performer in the KBW Bank Index. Dimon also said JPMorgan remains open to acquisitions and could potentially deploy $10 billion to $20 billion over the next couple of years, while the bank continues to compete in direct lending, where it has done about $20 billion of loans and still holds about $14 billion on its books. Nvidia (NVDA) reached $5.2 trillion with data-center revenue up 92% year over year, while Broadcom (AVGO) hit $2 trillion with AI revenue doubling annually. AI semiconductor companies are generating earnings growth faster than the broader market despite elevated valuations, allowing JPMorgan to project the S&P 500 could climb another 22% to 9,000 by mid-2027 as supply constraints enable stronger pricing power in memory chips. The analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 stocks and Micron Technology wasn't one of them. Get them here FREE. Everywhere investors look, the warning signs seem to be multiplying. Inflation ticked higher again in the latest Consumer Price Index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Producer prices are climbing, too, raising concerns companies may eventually pass those costs onto consumers. The University of Michigan’s consumer confidence index recently hit its lowest reading in 75 years. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 trades near historically elevated valuations after a massive run higher after last year’s April’s crash. So why does the stock market keep refusing to break? That question is becoming harder for bears to answer. Despite nonstop recession chatter and growing concerns that President Donald Trump’s bull market is running out of steam, not everyone thinks a crash is around the corner. In fact, according to a recent outlook from JPMorgan Private Bank, the S&P 500 could climb another 22% over the next year — potentially reaching 9,000 by mid-2027. That would mark another historic leg higher for the index. The core argument JPMorgan is making runs directly against the current mood on Wall Street. The bank acknowledges risks are building. Higher inflation, slowing consumer activity, and stretched valuations are all real concerns. Granted, the S&P 500 currently trades around 25 times forward earnings — well above its historical average closer to 17 or 18 times, according to FactSet data. Yet JPMorgan argues that every pullback is setting the market up for the next advance. That matters because investors have repeatedly expected this rally to collapse under the weight of higher interest rates, slowing growth, or geopolitical stress. Instead, each dip has become another buying opportunity. Importantly, JPMorgan does not call its 22% upside target the “base case” scenario. Rather, it describes the move as “entirely plausible” under a bullish economic and earnings backdrop. In other words, the firm is not predicting perfection — it is saying the conditions exist for another major rally if earnings growth keeps outpacing expectations. Surprisingly, much of that optimism comes down to one sector. According to JPMorgan, technology — particularly semiconductors tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure — remains the engine powering the broader market higher. Such a track record, with 14 consecutive years of dividend increases through various economic cycles, speaks volumes about the sustainability of its payout. For investors, a stable and growing dividend from a financial titan like JPMorgan Chase offers a tangible return on investment, particularly in an environment where income generation remains a priority. The current trailing twelve months (TTM) dividend payout for JPM stands at $6.00, translating to a dividend yield of 1.9% based on the current share price of $306.74. This yield, while slightly below the industry average of 2.3% as noted by some analysts, is underpinned by a conservative payout ratio of 29.2%, leaving ample room for future increases and reinvestment into the business. JPMorgan Chase's TTM dividend payout ratio of 29.2% is a critical metric that highlights the bank's prudent capital management and strong financial health. This ratio indicates that less than a third of the bank's earnings are distributed as dividends, leaving a substantial portion for reinvestment, debt reduction, or share repurchases. For a financial institution, a conservative payout ratio is particularly important as it provides a buffer against unexpected economic downturns and regulatory changes, ensuring the stability of future payouts. This conservative approach is further supported by JPM's robust earnings per share (EPS) of $21.12 for the trailing twelve months. With the $6.00 annualized dividend, the earnings comfortably cover the payout, reinforcing the sustainability of the dividend stream. In fact, Simply Wall St analysts project the dividend to remain well covered by earnings, with a forecast payout ratio of 28% in three years, even as EPS is expected to grow by 23% over the next three years. This forward-looking stability provides a strong foundation for income-seeking investors. Beyond the payout ratio, JPM's overall financial strength is evident in its substantial capital base. As of December 31, 2025, the firm reported $4.4 trillion in assets and $362 billion in stockholders' equity. Chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon has consistently emphasized the bank's "fortress balance sheet," which includes $291 billion in CET1 capital and $1.5 trillion in cash and marketable securities. This significant excess capital and robust liquidity enable the bank to not only sustain its dividend but also to navigate various market conditions, including the Federal Reserve's stress tests, which JPM has consistently cleared. JPMorgan Chase's capital allocation strategy extends beyond just dividends, encompassing significant share repurchase programs that further enhance shareholder value. On July 1, 2025, the firm's Board of Directors authorized a new common share repurchase program of $50 billion. This authorization, used at management's discretion, complements the dividend strategy by reducing the number of outstanding shares, thereby boosting EPS and potentially the stock price over time. The combination of a consistent dividend and an active share repurchase program signals a comprehensive approach to capital return. This dual strategy is particularly attractive to investors, as it offers both immediate income and potential capital appreciation. Jamie Dimon highlighted this, stating that the intended dividend increase and the new share repurchase program represent a "sustainable level of capital distribution" supported by strong financial performance. This commitment is crucial for maintaining investor confidence, especially given the firm's leadership position in investment banking, consumer banking, and asset management. Furthermore, JPM's strategic investments in its core businesses and expansion initiatives demonstrate a forward-looking approach to growth. The bank plans to open more than 500 new branches by 2027, with 150 already established in 2024, despite the rise of digital banking. This initiative, alongside its expansion of digital retail banking in Germany by early 2026 and across the European Union, aims to tailor its network to client needs and boost cross-selling. These growth drivers, coupled with a rebound in investment banking activity, are expected to underpin future earnings, providing a solid foundation for continued capital returns. JPMorgan Chase's current valuation metrics present a nuanced picture for investors, balancing its strong fundamentals with its recent stock performance. The stock is currently trading at $306.74, reflecting a modest gain of +0.12% today. Over the past year, JPM shares have traded within a 52-week range of $260.31 to $337.25, indicating that the stock is currently positioned towards the higher end of this range. From a valuation perspective, JPM's TTM Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 14.52. This is slightly below the industry average of 14.95x as noted by Zacks Investment Research in September 2025, suggesting that the stock might not be excessively overvalued compared to its peers. However, Simply Wall St noted in May 2026 that JPM's forward 12-month earnings multiple of 15.39x compared to the industry's 14.95x indicates a "stretched valuation." This discrepancy highlights the importance of considering both trailing and forward-looking metrics. Despite some concerns about valuation, analyst sentiment remains predominantly positive. Of 28 analysts covering JPM, 12 rate it a Buy, 14 a Hold, and only 2 a Sell. The average target price is $328.00, which implies a potential upside of approximately 7% from the current price. This consensus suggests that while the stock has performed well, there is still room for appreciation, driven by resilient credit quality, updated investor day guidance, and generally constructive views on large diversified banks. The firm's robust Return on Equity (ROE) of 16.3% and revenue growth of 3.3% (FY2025 YoY) further underscore its operational efficiency and ability to generate profits, making the current valuation potentially justifiable for long-term holders. While JPMorgan Chase presents a compelling investment case, particularly for dividend-focused investors, it is crucial to consider the inherent risks and future opportunities that could influence its performance. One significant opportunity lies in the rebound of its Investment Banking (IB) business. After a slowdown in global deal-making in early 2022 due to geopolitical tensions and inflation, JPM's total IB fees in the Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) segment rose 36% year-over-year in 2024. The healthy IB pipeline and an active M&A market are expected to drive stronger growth once macroeconomic conditions stabilize, with Douglas Petno, co-CEO of CIB, projecting low-double-digit year-over-year growth in IB fees for Q3 2025. However, the bank faces potential headwinds related to interest rate policy and net interest income (NII). While management projected NII of $95.5 billion for 2025, up more than 3% year-over-year, lower rates are expected to hurt the metric in 2026 as the Federal Reserve navigates rate policy. JPM's balance sheet is highly asset-sensitive, meaning declining rates could compress NII. This is a common challenge for large banks, with peers like Bank of America and Citigroup also anticipating modest NII compression over the medium term. On the risk side, asset quality deterioration remains a watch point. While JPM recorded negative provisions in 2021, a substantial rise in provisions occurred in subsequent years due to a worsening macroeconomic outlook. Management projects the card net charge-off rate to be 3.6% for 2025. However, lower rates could support asset quality by easing debt-service burdens and improving borrower solvency. JPM's extensive suite of services, from consumer banking to wealth management, diversifies its revenue streams, strengthening its resilience against sector-specific downturns and providing a buffer against these risks. JPMorgan Chase's consistent dividend declarations, including the latest $1.50 per share payout on July 31, 2026, underscore its financial strength and commitment to shareholders. The bank's conservative payout ratio of 29.2% and robust capital position provide a solid foundation for sustainable income. While valuation requires careful consideration, JPM's strategic growth initiatives and diversified business model position it well to navigate future economic shifts and continue delivering value. JP Morgan Asset Management is winding down its flagship US real estate income and growth fund, marking the end of the core-plus fund’s 24-year run. According to a JP Morgan spokesperson, after careful consideration, JP Morgan Asset Management has decided to wind down the JP Morgan US Real Estate Income and Growth Fund. “As a fiduciary, we believe this decision is in the best interests of the fund’s investors,” the spokesperson added. “We expect this process will take time, and we will proceed thoughtfully and deliberately, with a continued focus on maximising value through the process.” The US Real Estate Income and Growth Fund is a 2002-vintage vehicle that held $1.4bn (€1.2bn) in assets as of late 2025, according to a board meeting document from Ohio Bureau of Workers’ Compensation’s real estate consultant Meketa Investment. Meketa disclosed that the liquidation process is projected to take up to three years. Institutional investors in the fund include the Ohio Bureau of Workers’ Compensation, with a $40.7m exposure, and the North Dakota State Investment Board, which held an investment valued at $173.2m as of June 2025. The fund, which holds 84% of its assets in industrial and multifamily properties with the rest in office and retail, posted a net return of -1.9% for the three-month period and -9.7% over three years, the meeting document disclosed.
